title: Blood Parasite Microscopy

references.label: WHO Laboratory Quality Management System Handbook

summary: Certain parasites (notably malaria-causing Plasmodium species and some other blood-borne parasites) are diagnosed by direct microscopic examination of stained blood films, using the laboratory's existing peripheral smear technique with parasite-specific reading practices.
explanation: Thick blood films concentrate red cells (lysed during staining) into a small area, increasing sensitivity for detecting low-level parasitemia, while thin blood films preserve intact red cell and parasite morphology needed for species identification and parasitemia quantification — the two film types are complementary, not interchangeable, and both are prepared and stained (typically with a Romanowsky-type stain, as in the laboratory's existing peripheral smear technique) from the same specimen. Systematic examination of a sufficient number of fields under oil immersion is required before a negative result is reported, since low parasitemia can be missed on a cursory scan; a single negative film does not exclude infection, and repeat films over time are often part of the ordering clinician's protocol for a clinically suspicious case.

comparison.left: Concentrates parasites; higher sensitivity for detection
comparison.right: Morphology distorted; not used for species ID

comparison.left: Preserves morphology; used for species identification and quantification
comparison.right: Lower sensitivity for very low parasitemia

commonMisconceptions: Treating a single blood film read as definitively excluding parasitemia — a negative single film in a clinically suspicious case is generally followed by repeat films, per the ordering clinician's protocol.
